In A Sea Of EVs, Driving This 1989 Mercedes W124 Was The Perfect Palate Cleanser

ER
By Elena Rostova Global Automotive Industry & Supply-Chain Analyst • via Carscoops Wire

Source & Photography: Carscoops Wire Dispatch Verified Editorial Asset

⚡ EDITORIAL TAKE • ELENA ROSTOVA Global Automotive Industry & Supply-Chain Analyst

Capital Allocation Across Global Automakers

From an institutional perspective, the economic figures outlined in this dispatch from Carscoops reflect monumental shifts in automotive capital. Legacy original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and agile EV startups alike must balance heavy gigafactory capital expenditures against fluctuating consumer demand and trade tariffs. Supply chain resilience—especially across lithium, cathode precursor materials, and semiconductors—is determining profitability.

Big Picture: Upcoming quarterly delivery reports and operating margins will indicate which manufacturers are successfully navigating the EV transformation curve.

Modern cars may pack more power and more gadgets, but driving a restored '80s-era Mercedes shows how today's cars are lacking one thing: character

📌 The Core Development

With over 120 years of history, many arguments can be made for what constitutes peak automobile. I suppose it greatly depends on what criteria you're judging on. In terms of mass production, you have the Ford Model T , and cars like the VW Beetle, Fiat 500, and Citroën 2CV all come under consideration for their efforts to mobilize the masses. Then, from a purely technological and engineering standpoint, it'll be hard to top cars like the McLaren F1 and Bugatti Chiron.

But narrow it down to build quality and sheer over-engineering, and, for many, the car to jump into the forefront of one's mind is the Mercedes-Benz W124. If not peak automobile, this generation of E-Class certainly deserves the mantle of peak Mercedes-Benz. Driving new machinery these days, which is unavoidably dominated by EVs, can make you yearn for days of old. A time when the three-box sedan was considered the ultimate status symbol, and not a mildly raised SUV that would balk at the sight of wet grass.

🔍 Background & Sector Context

The W124 hails from a time before aspiration got the better of us. Yes, the three-pointed star meant a lot, but there was substance behind it. An overarching feeling of quality that, even four decades later, remains patently obvious to anyone who gets behind the wheel of one. And thanks to a friend who owned a 1989 pre-facelift 300E with the 12-valve 3.0-liter straight-six engine, I had the opportunity to experience the W124 firsthand. Forget badge snobbery — this car is the perfect palate cleanser for anyone who's lost sight of what truly matters in automobiles.

The W124 had an unenviable task ahead of itself: replace the already world-beating W123. The design team was headed by a young Italian by the name of Bruno Sacco, who had already made an impact with the "baby Benz" 190E. Creating the W124 took eight years of development, and it spawned multiple body styles, including sedan, estate, coupe, convertible, long-wheel-base limos, and even special-purpose shells that were used for applications such as ambulances and hearses.

📊 Industry & Real-World Impact

Being introduced in the late 1984 as a 1985 model, the W124 survived two facelifts, with the last convertibles being produced as late as 1997. German production of the sedan ended in 1995 as the W210 was introduced, but complete knock-down production (CKD) continued in India until 1997. That's a staggering 13-year lifecycle, which is unheard of today unless you're talking about the 16-year-old Dodge Durango . By comparison the W210 that replaced the W124 only lasted seven years of production. Beyond its initial run as a Mercedes, the W124 body style later found life in Korea, made under license as the SsangYong Chairman — albeit borrowing some bits from the W140 S-Class, an extended wheelbase, and a redesigned exterior — which ran until 2014.

🔮 Strategic Outlook & What Lies Ahead

Now, I'll be the first to admit, I initially never got the hype around the W124. To me, it felt too old-school, with a whiff of old hat. And up until this point, I had only ever driven the wheezy 2.0-liter four-cylinder petrol and diesel models that had left me rather underwhelmed. By comparison, the Bavarian-based competition came guns blazing with their E34-generation five series. While the 518is felt similarly underpowered, the 520i and 525i versions harnessed the power of a straight six engine, with later models introducing variable valve timing. These advances gave BMW's take on the mid-sized exec noticeably more grunt.

BMW was also ahead in the tech race, too. The E34 was available with some remarkable options for the time from the factory, including parking sensors, an auto-dimming rear-view mirror, electric sunshade, 16-button on-board computer (which displayed things like fuel consumption and range), and various other things that were just unheard of even in the most fully loaded W124 models. Combine these things with just how dialed in the chassis on those E34s were (steering box notwithstanding), and a younger me would have struggled to look twice at a Mercedes. However, in the cold light of the electric car revolution, combined with every brand losing its individuality, sitting behind the wheel of this article's featured car has me rethinking my dismissal of the W124. To put this car into context, it received a minor restoration over the last 12 months with the mechanicals having undergone a comprehensive refresh, but, overall, it retains the patina that 37 years does to a car.
